newsitem.title: ITALY: Will Marzotto merger escape "holding" tag?.
newsitem.headline: Will Marzotto merger escape "holding" tag?.

text.p: A planned merger of Italian textile group Marzotto and HPI has posed a difficult question for analysts: is it a marriage made in heaven or the birth of another ugly Italian industrial holding company?

Marzotto announced plans late last week to merge with newly-formed HPI. Although the merger was first greeted with enthusiasm, analysts now have reservations on how the market will eventually value the new company.

Marzotto is set to merge with Holding Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI), which itself has been spun off from industrial holding group Gemina, to form a new company to be called Gruppo Industriale Marzotto (GIM).
The new grouping will have two thirds of its sales in textiles and one third in publishing, and a string of stakes in a number of seemingly unrelated quoted companies.
"There is industrial logic to the merger, but the really good synergies only involve around 23 percent of the new group's aggregrate turnover," said Paul Gordon, analyst at IMI Sigeco.
These included Marzotto's clothing business being linked with HPI's GFT business, which produces clothes for top designer labels such as Armani and Prada.

Other analysts said the positive aspect of the merger could be the synergies achieved without paying hefty goodwill in a full-blow takeover. But they wondered if the market would value the group as a diverse industrial holding group, which usually trade at a discount of 20 percent to their net asset values.
Share markets generally rated publishing shares with their low capital intensity and large market shares higher than companies in the fragmented textile industry, they said.
This means the new group's share price could be lower than if the textile and publishing arms traded separately, thus losing overall shareholding value.

The merger brings together Marzotto's clothing business, its materials and yarns business and a majority holding in German clothing label Hugo Boss, with HPI's CFT business and its majority holding in sportswear group Fila, whose shares are quoted in New York.

Marie-Christine Keith, Italian equities analyst with HSBC James Capel in London, sees the logic of the merger. The fact that Pietro Marzotto was to remain chairman of the enlarged group was good news as he was a well respected figure, she said.
But she too was concerned over the new company being labelled a holding company, and she calculated the net asset value of the new group's share at 14,637 lire ($8.65) per ordinary share.

Marzotto shares leapt over six percent on Monday after the merger was announced and hit a record high on March 11 of 15,210 lire. On Thursday, the shares traded down 2.54 percent at 14,000 lire in a generally lower Milan share market.

Analysts said the new management's hands would be tied over HPI's interest in the nation's number two publishing house Rizzoli Corriere della Sera (RCS), which includes Italy's top selling mainstream daily paper Corriere della Sera.
"It would make sense to sell off the publishing side, but that seems unlikely given the old problems at RCS and the prestige of owning a publisher," said another Milan analyst.

A so-called Super Gemina plan was hatched in late 1995 to fold Gemina's interests into the then-named Ferruzzi Finanziaria but it was abandoned after the discovery of huge losses at RCS. The deal was orchestrated by Milan's top merchant bank Mediobanca, which is also behind this latest Marzotto merger.
"This deal clearly makes more sense than Super Gemina, which was understood by few outside Mediobanca, but how will the market see it in the clear light of day?" asked the analyst. ($1=1,692 lire)
